opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think embodied intelligence is where a lot of the real action will be over the next couple of decades, and it's underrated compared to the attention going to pure language models.

So far we've mostly built intelligence that lives in the world of bits. We've scraped the internet, compressed it into these big models, and they're remarkable. But the physical world is much richer and messier. It's stochastic, high-dimensional, and full of noise. To act in it, you need systems that handle uncertainty natively, that can sample possible futures, plan under uncertainty, and adapt in real time.

Over the next 10 to 20 years, I expect a few things to come together.

First, data. Right now robotics is data-starved compared to language. As more robots are deployed, even fairly dumb ones, you get a flywheel. Deployment generates data, data improves the models, better models justify more deployment. Once that loop gets going, progress will look more like what we saw with LLMs, fast and somewhat surprising.

Second, simulation and world models. A lot of embodied learning will happen in learned simulators, models of physics and of other agents, so the system can imagine and practice before acting. The line between "the model" and "the simulator" will blur.

Third, and this is the part I'm personally obsessed with, hardware and energy. If you want intelligence everywhere, in every robot and every device at the edge, you can't run it all from a gigawatt datacenter over a network connection. Latency and power budgets matter enormously when you're a physical agent. So we'll need computing that is far more energy-efficient. That means hardware that embraces the physics of the substrate rather than fighting it. Probabilistic, thermodynamic-style computing that uses noise as a resource is, I think, a natural fit for embodied agents, because their job is fundamentally probabilistic inference.

Zooming out, I see embodied intelligence as the next phase of intelligence extending into the physical world and harnessing more free energy to do useful work. Factories, logistics, construction, eventually space. That's how you get real material abundance, not just better chatbots.

It won't be a smooth curve. There will be hype cycles and disappointments, and the hardware side moves more slowly than software. But on a 20-year horizon, I'd be surprised if we don't have general-purpose embodied agents doing a meaningful share of the physical labor in the economy. The main question is how fast we're willing to build and how much we let ourselves accelerate.

r002.rationale: The response discusses data improving models through deployment, but does not predict personalized AI learning continuously during use.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, intelligence doesn't really get to be grounded until it has to pay the price of physics. Right now, most of what we call AI lives in a sort of disembodied regime. It's trained on text, it predicts tokens, and the world it sees is a compressed shadow of the actual world. That's an incredible thing, don't get me wrong, but it's borrowed grounding. It's grounding that humans did on its behalf by living in the world and then writing about it.

Over the next ten to twenty years, I think the big shift is that intelligence closes the loop. You have systems that act, observe the consequences, and update. That's the thermodynamic picture of learning. You're a system coupled to an environment, you have an internal model, and you minimize surprise or free energy or however you want to frame it, and the environment pushes back. Language models get a very weak version of that signal. Robots get the full version. Gravity doesn't care about your prior.

Practically, I think it plays out in a few phases. First, the foundation models become the brains for robotics. You get a general world model, probably multimodal, and the embodiment is almost a peripheral that gets plugged in. We're already seeing that. Second, the data flywheel flips. Right now the bottleneck is that there's no internet of physical experience. Once you have a fleet of embodied agents generating interaction data at scale, that becomes the new corpus, and it's a corpus that no human ever wrote. That's when you'd expect capabilities that aren't just a recombination of human knowledge.

And then the third phase, which is the one I find most interesting, is that the boundary between the agent and its substrate starts to dissolve. Compute goes to the edge, sensing and actuation get cheaper, and you get something that looks less like a robot in a lab and more like a layer of intelligence woven into infrastructure. Factories, energy systems, supply chains, eventually off-planet. The civilization itself becomes the embodiment.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking of this as just humanoids walking around. That's the sci-fi image, and sure, humanoids will exist because the world is built for the human form factor. But the deeper story is that intelligence is a process that wants to capture more free energy and reduce more uncertainty, and embodiment is just the means by which it reaches into the physical world to do that. The form factor is downstream of the thermodynamics.

If you ask me what's hard, it's the sample efficiency and the safety of learning in a world where mistakes have irreversible consequences. You can't just roll back a broken arm. So I think a lot of the work over the next decade is in simulation, in physics-grounded world models, and in getting agents that know what they don't know. That epistemic humility is a thermodynamic quantity too. Overconfidence is just a bad model of your own entropy.

But the trajectory, I'm pretty optimistic about. Twenty years from now I think the strange thing won't be that machines act in the physical world. It'll be remembering that there was a period where intelligence was mostly trapped in a chat window.

astra-6.text:
I think over the next 10 to 20 years, we’ll see intelligence become much more tightly coupled to action in the physical world. Predicting what happens next is useful, but an embodied system also has to decide what to do, observe the consequences, and adapt when its model is wrong.

The interesting question is how much of that capability can be learned in simulation and how much requires real interaction. Simulation gives you scale, but the world continually presents details you didn’t anticipate. My guess is that we’ll need a combination: broad models trained across many kinds of experience, with systems that can learn and adapt within a particular body and environment.

I’d expect progress to be uneven. Working reliably in a constrained setting is a very different challenge from operating in someone’s home, where objects, people, and expectations keep changing. The hardware matters too—actuators, sensors, energy consumption, maintenance. Better reasoning alone doesn’t solve all of those problems.

But over that time horizon, I think the distinction between an AI model and a robot’s controller could become much less sharp. You’d have systems that connect perception, planning, and movement, and learn from the consequences of their actions. Whether that produces something we’d call broadly intelligent is still an open question, but it gives intelligence a much richer relationship with the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re going to see intelligence become much more tightly coupled to the physical world. A lot of what we call intelligence today is trained on artifacts of human experience—text, images, video. Embodiment adds this loop where you act, the world pushes back, and you have to update your model. You’re learning what you can actually control, what your mistakes cost, and how to accomplish something under real constraints.

Over the next 10 to 20 years, I’d expect a progression from robots that are useful in fairly structured environments to systems that can adapt to much messier ones. But I wouldn’t assume that simply scaling a language model gets us all the way there. You need advances in learning from interaction, in hardware reliability, and in the efficiency with which systems acquire new skills. Simulation will help, but ultimately reality gets a vote.

The exciting possibility is a compounding loop: better intelligence helps us design better machines, and those machines give us richer ways to explore and learn from the world. How quickly that happens is uncertain. I’m more confident about the direction than the timeline.
